newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines sets sights high after APEC.
newsitem.headline: Philippines sets sights high after APEC.

text.p: The Philippines, the former "sick man of Asia" now basking in its role as host of the annual Asia-Pacific summit, is setting its sights on becoming a regional financial centre.
"We are going to go for it," a jubilant Philippine Financial Secretary Roberto de Ocampo told Reuters on Friday.

He said most of the ingredients were already in place for the Philippines to act as a financial hub for the booming region, whose foreign and trade ministers are currently meeting in Manila ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum summit on Monday.
A wide range of reforms introduced under President Fidel Ramos has opened up an economy that for decades was heavily protected from both foreign and domestic competition.

They have been credited with transforming the Philippines' economic landscape, ending inefficient monopolies in telecommunications and air transport and spurring complacent local firms to new competitive endeavours.

From virtually flat growth when Ramos took office in 1992, government planners say growth this year is likely to be a respectable 7.0 percent-plus while millions of dollars worth of foreign investment has been flooding in.

Some of the most crucial reforms have been in the financial sector, particularly banking where Philippine liberalisation has gone further and faster than almost any other country in the region, economists say.
Other reforms have opened up other financial services, foreign exchange dealing and insurance.
De Ocampo said the passage on Thursday of a crucial new tax law would also add to the Philippines' credibility and demonstrate to the world that the reform process was not a flash in the pan.
"It's a tiding of comfort and joy," de Ocampo said of the new excise tax law which Ramos signed on Friday.
"It was very timely in the sense that having the APEC here we have the eyes of the world on us," he said.
De Ocampo said the final version of the law was very close to the original bill proposed by the government.
Private economists and international financial institutions had all warned that passage of new laws to eradicate widespread tax evasion was crucial to the government reform process.
Ramos himself said in a speech that the new tax law, passed in the face of a dogged rearguard action by its powerful opponents, would help propel the Philippines into "the Big League".

The large-circulation Manila Bulletin also felt that becoming a regional financial centre was not as far-fetched as it might seem to people who usually associate the Philippines with political turmoil, natural disasters and plain incompetence.
Apart from a legislative framework, the Philippines has a large, well-trained workforce and growing expertise in the information technology essential to any ambitions as a financial hub.
"All told, the road to becoming a financial centre for the Asia-Pacific region seems pretty well paved," it said.
